facts.text: The Paiwan people live in southern Taiwan, on both sides of Dawu Mountain and in the southern Central Mountain Range, in Pingtung and Taitung.
Pottery pots, glass beads, and bronze knives are known as the three treasures of the Paiwan.
A Paiwan legend says the ancestors made glass beads from the eyes of dragonflies, so the beads are regarded as gifts from the gods.
Traditionally, glass beads marked high status and only nobles could keep them.
Glass beads were family heirlooms passed down through generations and important betrothal or dowry gifts, especially in marriages between chiefs and nobles.
Important beads have their own names and stories, such as the sun's tear and the bead of the clouded leopard, now also called the peacock bead.
The peacock bead stands for love and is linked to legends of love.
Today, Paiwan glass beads are made by hand in workshops: the glass is heated over a flame, and a bead held too far from the flame cools and can crack.
Making a bead in a workshop session takes about 1 to 1.5 hours.
